question.text:
Consider the vector space $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ of all $2 \times 2$ matrices over $\mathbb{R}.$

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &2 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$ is a linearly independent set in $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$
  2. $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &2 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$
  3. $\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &2 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$ is a basis of $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$
question.explanation:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation \[ x_1 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + x_2 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &2 \end{bmatrix}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix} \] is true if and only if $x_1=x_2=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, \[ \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = 3 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + (-1) \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &2 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

  • Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 4 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ can't be written as a linear combination of \[ \bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &2 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\} \] since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry $a_{11} = 0\mathbin{:}$ \[ a \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + b \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &2 \end{bmatrix}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ a & 2b \end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

example.title: Identifying True Statements About Sets of Vectors in a Matrix Vector Space

question.text:
Consider the vector space $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ of all $2 \times 2$ matrices over $\mathbb{R}.$

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$ is a linearly independent set in $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$
  2. $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4 \end{bmatrix}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$
  3. $\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$ is a basis of $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$
question.explanation:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation \[ x_1 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + x_2 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}} + x_3 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}}= \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix} \] is true if and only if $x_1=x_2=x_3=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, \[ \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4 \end{bmatrix} = 2 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + (-4) \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}} + 3 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

  • Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ can't be written as a linear combination of \[ \bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\} \] since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry $a_{21} = 0\mathbin{:}$ \[ a \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + b \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}}+ c \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}} = \begin{bmatrix} a &c \\ 0 & b \end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

example.title: Identifying True Statements About Sets of Vectors in a Matrix Vector Space

question.text:
Let $\mathcal{B}= \big\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2} \big\}$ and $\mathcal{C}= \big\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2}, \mathbf{c_3} \big\}$ be bases of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3,$ respectively.

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\big\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2}, \mathbf{c_3}, \mathbf{x} \big\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$
  2. $\big\{ \mathbf{b_1}, 2\mathbf{b_2} \big\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$
  3. $\big\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2}, 2\mathbf{c_2} \big\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$
question.explanation:
Since $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

  • $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ are maximally linearly independent sets in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3,$ respectively, and

  • $\mathcal{B}$ spans $\mathbb{R}^2,$ while $\mathcal{C}$ spans $\mathbb{R}^3.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is false. Since $\mathcal{C}= \big\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2}, \mathbf{c_3} \big\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb R^3$, any vector of $\mathbb{R}^3,$ including the given vector $\mathbf{x},$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{c_1},$ $\mathbf{c_2},$ and $\mathbf{c_3}.$ This means that $\big\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2}, \mathbf{c_3}, \mathbf{x} \big\}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation \begin{align*} x_1(\mathbf{b}_1)+x_2(2\mathbf{b}_2) &= \mathbf{0} \\ \end{align*} is equivalent to \begin{align*} x_1\mathbf{b}_1+(2x_2)\mathbf{b}_2 &= \mathbf{0}, \end{align*} which, since $\left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ is linearly independent, gives \[ \begin{cases} x_1= 0\\ 2x_2=0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} x_1= 0\\ x_2=0. \end{cases} \] Also, $\big\{ \mathbf{b}_1, 2\mathbf{b}_2 \big\}$ spans $\mathbb{R}^2$ since any linear combination of $\mathcal{B}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\big\{ \mathbf{b}_1, 2\mathbf{b}_2 \big\}\mathbin{:}$ \[ x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2 = x_1\mathbf{b}_1+\dfrac{x_2}{2}(2\mathbf{b}_2) \]

  • Statement III is false. The set $\left\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2},2\mathbf{c_2} \right\}$ is not a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ because the third vector is a linear combination of $\mathbf{c_1}$ and $\mathbf{c_2}.$ This means that the set is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

example.title: Identifying True Statements About Bases of Abstract Vector Spaces

question.text:
Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ and $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2} \right\}$ be bases of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and $\mathbb{R}^2$, respectively.

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\left\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2}, \mathbf{x} \right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$
  2. $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2} \right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$
  3. $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{c_1} \right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$
question.choice1: None of the statements are true
question.explanation:
Since $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

  • $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ are maximally linearly independent sets in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3,$ respectively, and

  • $\mathcal{B}$ spans $\mathbb{R}^2,$ while $\mathcal{C}$ spans $\mathbb{R}^3.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is false. Since $\mathcal{C}= \big\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2} \big\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb R^2$, any vector of $\mathbb{R}^2,$ including the given vector $\mathbf{x},$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{c_1}$ and $\mathbf{c_2}.$ This means that $\big\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2}, \mathbf{x} \big\}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

  • Statement II is false. The set $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2} \right\}$ is not a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ because the vector $\mathbf{b_3}$ is in $\mathbb{R}^3$ but it is not a linear combination of $\mathbf{b_1}$ and $\mathbf{b_2}$ as the set $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly independent. This means that the set does not span $\mathbb{R}^3$ and therefore, cannot be a basis.

  • Statement III is false. The set $\big\{\mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{c_1} \big\}$ is not a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true".
